objectives: Run the byte-pair-encoding merge loop by hand
Explain the vocab-size vs sequence-length tradeoff

slides.title: Part 1 — Why BPE exists
slides.body: You proved the char-vs-word dilemma in the last lesson. Byte-Pair Encoding is the algorithm that resolves it — and it is almost startlingly simple for how load-bearing it is in every modern LLM.

slides.title: The compromise, made concrete
slides.body: BPE starts from the smallest *safe* units — bytes or characters, so **nothing is ever out-of-vocabulary** — and repeatedly performs one move: find the **most frequent adjacent pair** of current tokens across the corpus and **merge** it into a single new token, until the vocabulary reaches a target size. Outcomes by construction: high-frequency words coalesce into single tokens (cheap, semantic); rare words remain a few subword pieces (no `<unk>`, morphology preserved); never-seen input still encodes as bytes. **One** hyperparameter — target vocab size — slides between "few long tokens, big embedding table" and "many short tokens, long sequences."

slides.title: The merge-pair training loop
slides.body:
```
vocab ← all bytes/characters
merges ← []
while |vocab| < target:
    pairs ← count every adjacent token pair over the corpus
    best  ← argmax(pairs)            # most frequent adjacent pair
    vocab.add(concat(best))
    merges.append(best)              # ORDER matters
    rewrite corpus applying that one merge
```

The **ordered list of merges *is* the tokenizer.** Training is just "learn the merge list." Encoding new text re-applies the merges in the same order until none apply. There is no neural network and no gradient inside the tokenizer — it is pure corpus statistics, which is why it's fast, deterministic, and reproducible.

slides.title: Worked merge, fully by hand
slides.body: Corpus (word:count): `low:5  lower:2  newest:6  widest:3`. Represent each as chars + end-marker. Count adjacent pairs across all words weighted by count: the pair `e s` occurs in `newest`(6) and `widest`(3) → 9, `s t` similarly → 9, `l o` → 7, … Merge the top pair, say `e s`→`es`. Recount: now `es t` appears 9 times → merge → `est`. Continue: `est` becomes a single token shared by `newest` and `widest`; `low` stays cheap because `l o`,`lo w` were frequent. After $k$ merges you have a vocab of size (initial + $k$) and a fixed merge order. Notice the algorithm *discovered* the morpheme-like unit `est` purely from frequency — no linguistics input.

question.question: A BPE tokenizer trained on English meets the word `tokenization` for the first time. Most likely outcome?
options: Split into known subword pieces like `token` + `ization`
Split into single characters `t o k e n …`
Added to the vocabulary on the fly
question.explanation: BPE never emits `<UNK>`: every character is in the base vocab and any string is reachable by some merge sequence. Common subwords (`token`, `ization`) are already vocabulary entries, so the word decomposes cleanly into a few pieces.

question.question: Order these BPE training steps correctly (first → last).

items.label: Initialize vocab with all single characters
Count all adjacent symbol pairs in the corpus
Merge the single most frequent pair into a new token
Repeat until N merges are reached

question.explanation: BPE is: start from characters → count adjacent pairs → merge the most frequent pair → repeat. Each iteration grows the vocabulary by exactly one token (the new merge), so after N iterations the vocab is base_chars + N.

slides.title: Part 2 — The vocab-size tradeoff, in numbers
Bigger vocab ⇄ shorter sequences (quantified)
slides.body: More merges → longer average tokens → **fewer tokens per document** (shorter sequences) but a **larger** embedding matrix $E\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times d}$ and output projection. Concretely, going from 8k→50k vocab on English text typically cuts token count per document by a large fraction; since attention is $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$, a 25% shorter sequence is ~$0.75^2\approx 0.56\times$ the attention compute — a *bigger* win than the extra embedding rows cost. Push vocab too far and you get rare, under-trained token embeddings (each seen too seldom to learn well). Empirically English LLMs settle around 30k–100k; multilingual models go larger to cover many scripts.

slides.title: Leading spaces & number splits — now mechanistically explained
slides.body: Earlier you observed byte-level BPE attaching leading spaces and fragmenting numbers/code. Now the *cause* is precise: merges are chosen by adjacency frequency in a prose-dominated corpus. Space-then-word pairs are extremely frequent, so the space gets merged onto the word — giving the `" cat"`≠`"cat"` behavior. Digit pairs and code-symbol pairs are comparatively rare, so few merges form there and they stay shattered. The surface quirks are downstream of one line: *merge the most frequent pair*.

question.question: With a 50k-token English BPE vocab, ~how many tokens does a 1,000-word English document take?
options: ≈ 1,300 (about 0.75 words per token / ~4 chars per token)
question.explanation: The English BPE rule of thumb is ~0.75 words/token (~4 chars/token). Leading spaces, punctuation, and rare-word splits push 1,000 words to roughly 1,300 tokens — directly relevant to context-window budgeting and API cost.

slides.title: Part 3 — Variants you'll meet in real systems
WordPiece, Unigram, byte-level BPE
slides.body:
- **WordPiece** (BERT): same greedy spirit, but the merge criterion is *likelihood gain* of the corpus under a unigram LM, not raw pair frequency.
- **Unigram LM** (SentencePiece, T5): the inverse direction — start from a large candidate vocab and *prune* the tokens whose removal least hurts corpus likelihood; tokenization becomes probabilistic (multiple segmentations scored).
- **Byte-level BPE** (GPT-2 onward): run BPE over raw *bytes* rather than Unicode characters, so the 256 byte values are the base alphabet and *every possible string on Earth* is encodable with zero `<unk>` — the modern default for general LLMs.

Different objective functions, identical goal: a fixed-size vocab trading sequence length against coverage.

question.question: In 2–3 sentences, explain why BPE beats both word-level and character-level tokenization. Touch on vocabulary size, out-of-vocabulary handling, and sequence length.

rubricCriteria.description: BPE keeps a fixed-size vocabulary (vs unbounded word-level)
BPE handles unseen words by decomposing into subwords (no <UNK>)
BPE sequences are shorter than character-level for the same text

question.explanation: A strong answer: BPE fixes the vocabulary size (unlike word-level, which is unbounded and produces <UNK> on unseen words); it represents any word by composing known subword pieces, so there is no out-of-vocabulary failure; and its sequences are far shorter than character-level for the same text, which keeps the O(n²) attention cost manageable.

slides.title: BPE as an optimization, stated
slides.body: BPE is a greedy approximation to: *choose a vocabulary of size $|V|$ minimizing the expected number of tokens per corpus document.* Exact minimization is combinatorial; BPE's greedy "merge the most frequent pair" is the tractable heuristic, and it works remarkably well in practice. slides.title: Part 5 — Edge cases & a counter-intuitive production bug
Smaller vocab can make inference *slower*
slides.body: A natural "optimization" — shrink the vocab to reduce the embedding table and save memory — can *increase* latency. Mechanism: fewer merges → longer token sequences → quadratically more attention compute, which dominates the modest embedding-table savings. This is the kind of second-order effect that separates someone who memorized "BPE merges pairs" from someone who understands the cost model. Work through it:

question.question: Diagnose the latency regression.
question.scenario: To save memory you shrink the BPE vocabulary from 50k to 8k. Inference latency goes UP, not down.

rubricCriteria.description: a smaller vocab means fewer merges → longer token sequences
transformer compute scales with sequence length (attention is ~O(n^2))
the longer sequences outweigh the smaller embedding table → net slower

question.explanation: Vocab size trades embedding-table size against sequence length. Too small a vocab lengthens every sequence, and attention cost grows with length.

hints: How does token count per sentence change?
slides.workedSolution: A larger vocab has more merges, so text encodes into fewer, longer tokens (shorter sequences) — paid for with a larger embedding and output projection.

question.explanation: More merges → longer tokens → fewer tokens per text (shorter sequences) at the cost of a bigger embedding/output matrix.

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body: You can run BPE by hand, explain every production quirk from the single merge rule, and reason quantitatively about the vocab↔length↔cost triangle. The pipeline is now complete through *input representation*. Next the model finally computes: **softmax** — the universal head turning scores into a probability distribution and the core of attention weights — then attention itself.
